<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-author">Author</button></h2><div id="work-acc-author" class="accordion-collapse collapse show"><div class="accordion-body"><p class="mb-0 work-author"><a href="../poets/viranandi.html">Vīranandi / वीरनन्दि</a></p></div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Candraprabhacarita is an epic poem that tells the story of Candraprabha, the eighth Tīrthaṅkara or enlightened being of Jainism. The poem begins with the birth of Candraprabha, the son of King Mahāsena and Queen Lakṣmaṇa of Ayōdhyā. At a young age, Candraprabha renounces his royal status and becomes a Jain monk, dedicating himself to pursuing spiritual knowledge and enlightenment.<br>Throughout the poem, Candraprabha faces various challenges and trials, including battles with demons and temptations from the god of love. Still, ultimately, he remains steadfast in his devotion to the Jain path. He is known for his compassion and wisdom, and he teaches others about the importance of nonviolence and the pursuit of enlightenment.<br>Candraprabhacarita is notable for its vivid descriptions of the natural world, its exploration of Jain philosophy and ethics, and its highly literary style. The poem has been celebrated for centuries within the Jain community as a masterpiece of religious literature. It continues to be studied and revered by scholars of Sanskrit and Jainism.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Candraprabhacarita is divided into 18 cantos or chapters and include the following:<br>Invocation<br>i. Description of Ayōdhyā and the birth of Candraprabha<br>ii. The childhood of Candraprabha and his decision to become a monk<br>iii. The renunciation of Candraprabha and his training with Jain teachers<br>iv. The story of Candraprabha's enlightenment<br>v. The teachings of Candraprabha on non-violence and compassion<br>vi. Candraprabha's travels and the story of the demon Vidyutprabhā<br>vii. Candraprabha's meeting with the god of love and his rejection of worldly pleasures<br>viii. Candraprabha's encounter with the demon Madanavega<br>ix. Candraprabha's battle with the demon Mura<br>x. Candraprabha's visit to the court of King Sudarśana<br>xi. The story of Candraprabha's past lives<br>xii. Candraprabha's teachings on karma and the nature of the universe<br>xiii. Candraprabha's encounter with the god Varuṇa and the story of the demon Vyāghra<br>xiv. Candraprabha's journey to the heavenly realms<br>xv. The story of the demon Tāraka and Candraprabha's battle with him<br>xvi. Candraprabha's visit to the kingdom of the Yakṣas<br>xvii. The story of the demon Kālakētu and Candraprabha's final victory over him<br>xviii. Conclusion and praise of Candraprabha</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Candraprabhacarita, is an epic poem devoted entirely to the life of Candraprabha, the eighth Tīrthaṅkara or enlightened being of Jainism, and offers a detailed account of his teachings and exploits. This focus on a single Jain figure is unusual in Sanskrit literature, which more often deals with Hindu gods and heroes.<br>Candraprabhacarita is praised for its philosophical depth and its exploration of Jain doctrine and ethics. The poem deals with complex concepts such as karma, the nature of the universe, and the attainment of enlightenment, and presents them in a clear and accessible way. The teachings of Candraprabha on nonviolence and compassion are particularly noteworthy, and have had a lasting impact on Jain thought and practice.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Candraprabhacarita is a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature. The epic poem is notable for its literary style, vivid descriptions, and philosophical depth, and is considered one of the most important works in Jain literature and Sanskrit literature more broadly. Candraprabhacarita is praised for its poetic beauty and its skilful use of language. The poem's descriptions of the natural world, celestial realms, and battle scenes are particularly vivid and powerful, and demonstrate Vīranandi's mastery of Sanskrit poetry. The language of the poem is rich and elegant, and its use of metaphor and simile adds to its overall beauty and impact.<br>In addition to its literary qualities, Candraprabhacarita is also a significant contribution to Sanskrit literature for its philosophical depth and its exploration of Jain doctrine and ethics. The poem deals with complex concepts such as karma, the nature of the universe, and the attainment of enlightenment, and presents them in a clear and accessible way. The teachings of Candraprabha on non-violence and compassion are particularly noteworthy, and have had a lasting impact on Jain thought and practice.<br><br>In addition to its unique style and contribution to Sanskrit literature, the Candraprabhacarita is notable for its historical context. It was written during the reign of the Cālukya dynasty, which was one of the most powerful and influential dynasties in South India during the medieval period. The Cālukyas were known for their patronage of the arts and their support of Jainism, which is reflected in the Candraprabhacarita. The work also contains references to various other religious and philosophical traditions, including Buddhism and Advaita Vedānta, demonstrating the author's familiarity with diverse intellectual and spiritual currents of the time. Overall, the Candraprabhacarita remains an important work of literature and a valuable source of historical and cultural information about medieval India.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-quotations">Quotable Quotations</button></h2><div id="work-acc-quotations" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">1\. क्षणभङ्गुरवृत्तिजीवितं भवभाजामिति नात्र विस्मयः । तदिहाद्भुतमेतदीदृशं यदर्वस्यद्भिरपि प्रमुह्यते ॥ \[चन्द्रप्रभचरितम् - १.६७\]<br>kṣaṇabhaṅguravṛttijīvitaṃ bhavabhājāmiti nātra vismayaḥ । <br>tadihādbhutametadīdṛśaṃ yadarvasyadbhirapi pramuhyate ॥ \[candraprabhacaritam - 1.67\]</div></div></div>
